newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-WEEK AHEAD-U.S. rate speculation to dominate.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-WEEK AHEAD-U.S. rate speculation to dominate.

text.p: The surprise weakening in United States employment data, and perhaps the wider economy, is set to dominate Australian financial markets this week, overshadowing bullish local rates comments by Treasurer Peter Costello.

Even so, his "Santa Claus" reference last Friday about a possible cut in local interest rates later this year, along with his controversial comments about U.S. economic direction, will be the focus of attention for politicians in Canberra when the current session of parliament resumes on Tuesday.

After the close of local trade last Friday, the United States Commerce Department released its highly-sensitive monthly payrolls data which showed a surprise fall of 40,000 in September non-farm payrolls.

This was the first decline since January. Just as importantly, the data shocked markets and forecasters who had predicted a rise of about 175,000 and who had believed the Federal Reserve Board would raise interest rates sooner rather than later, but after the November presidential election.
U.S. unemployment also rose slightly to 5.2 from 5.1 percent in August.

The September data pushed U.S. financial markets higher across the board, including the rate-sensitive U.S. dollar, as investors did a 180 degree turn and now speculated on how long the Fed would keep steady, rather than increase, interest rates.
Wall Street jumped 60 points to end at a record high while the key 30 year bond yield dropped to 6.49 percent.
Apart from the resumption of Parliament, local markets will also watch September employment data and August housing finance, both to be released on Thursday.

Another job-based activity indicator, the ANZ job vacancies figure for September, will be released on Monday even though the key Sydney market will be closed for Labour Day. Credit markets will trade on SYCOM but stocks and currencies will be traded as usual, although turnover will be very light.
AUSTRALIAN BONDS (Fri 10-yr cash yield 7.59, 3-yr 6.96)

Local credit markets face a hectic week, with the most likely influence being the implications arising from the shock decline in U.S. September non-farm payrolls. The 40,000 decline was in sharp contract to the predictions of another steep increase about about 175,000 after a strong rise in August.

What had been confident speculation about when the U.S. central bank would hike rates, not if, was turned on its head with economists now saying the Federal Reserve will at least keep rates steady in the near future, and a cut might not be out of the question.

As local bonds had already been rising on speculation of another cut in Australian rates, the impetus provided by the U.S. speculation could nudge yields even lower. However, traders said the greatest price gains might already have been seen.

Macquarie Bank said the local rates sentiment was spurred by Treasurer Peter Costello's comments in New York last Friday which alluded to further rate cuts both this year and next year -- the "Santa Claus" statement.
The investment bank said the next rate cut was likely after the Reserve Bank of Australia's next monthly board meeting on November 5 and could be in the order of about 50 basis points to 6.5 percent.

Westpac economists said Thursday's local release of September labour force data will reinforce the argument for another cut in the official cash rate. While adjusted unemployment could fall a tick to 8.7 percent in September due to participation rate factors, Westpac said total adjusted employment could fall by up to 15,000 against the 37,900 gain in August.
AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR (Fri US$0.7896/01, New York US$7886/91)

The Australian dollar will most likely remain in a nervous one U.S. cent trading range this week, but tend towards the upside of US$0.7950 as investors and traders come to grips with the implications of the United States payrolls data for September.
The surprise fall in non-farm payrolls stopped speculation of a near-term Fed rate rise dead in its track.

Economists now believe the Fed will hold rates steady for quite a while, which could increase the appeal of the Australian dollar which often trades based on international interest rate differentials.

But if the payrolls data is the precursor of wider signs of a slowing U.S. economy, then the drag-on effect for the local currency could see it head south at a rate of knots as demand for commodities weakens and Australian exporters struggle to find alternative markets.
AUSTRALIAN STOCKS (Fri: All Ordinaries 2,315.5, up 0.6)
The Wall Street surge last Friday should be at least partly reflected by Australian stocks this week, although serious trading will not begin until Tuesday due to the Sydney holiday.

Driven by the weak U.S. September non-farm payrolls data, the Dow index gained 60 points to a record 5,993 -- nearing the 6,000 milestone which should prove goods news for Bill Clinton in next month's presidential election.

U.S. bonds also rose on the payrolls result, adding to the positive tone for stock traders and investors but on later reflection they both cautioned that the figure will hopefully not indicate a serious weakening in U.S. economic growth.

"In general the U.S. market is likely to continue its rise in the lead up to the presidential election and the Australian market should be carried along in its wake," said Jim Tredenick, a dealer at Brisbane broker, Nevitts.
Tredenick said that investors had discounted the likelihood of a rate cut in the near term.
"I don't think the local employment data (to be released next Thursday) even if it is weak, will be enough to rekindle the type of speculation we saw earlier this week," he said.

A large number of company's go ex-dividend this week with Thursday the worst affected day with no less than 20 stocks changing the basis of their quotation including Santos Ltd, Westfield Holdings Ltd, National Foods Ltd and Henry Walker Group Ltd.
Profit-taking late last week, particularly in the bank sector appeared to come to an end on Friday, dealers said.
Consequently further upside was seen for banks this week particularly if Australian employment data to be released on Thursday supports a local interest rate cut.
In terms of company news Golden Shamrock Mines Ltd shareholders vote on a merger proposal with major Ghana gold group Ashanti Goldfields.
Annual meetings next week include Commonwealth Bank of Australia in Melbourne on Tuesday, Jupiters Ltd at its casino on the Gold Coast on Thursday and G.E. Crane Holdings Ltd in Sydney on Friday. .
Share market investors like other market traders will be watching Thursday's release of employment data on Thursday.
Dealers said a sharp movement in reaction to the data by the Australian bond market was likely to be mirrored by the bourse.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
